title: Micro-acknowledgement protocol for partial outputs and SDK liveness
body:
Context:

This doc proposes a lightweight client-server micro-acknowledgement protocol for the Hosted API streaming surface. The goal is to give clients a low-friction signal channel that:
- lets the service know how far the client has consumed streamed partial outputs (progress)
- allows the runtime to safely and proactively prefetch model prefixes / KV cache and trigger speculative tool calls
- improves SDK liveness handling (detecting stalled clients, enabling graceful fallback)
- surfaces telemetry that ties consumption patterns to token-level cost and latency

Why a new protocol?
Today's streaming primitives are one-way: server -> client. That leaves the runtime blind to whether a partial result was observed, truncated, or ignored. Consequences: wasted prefetching, missed speculative opportunities, difficulty enforcing low-latency SLOs for interactive clients, and brittle SDK heuristics.

Design principles
- Minimal: a few small ack types (strings) and optional numeric offsets, cheap to emit from mobile/edge clients.
- Opportunistic: acks are best-effort—lossy network shouldn't break correctness. Server still provides final canonical output and must support idempotency.
- Privacy and safety: ack payloads contain only positional/consumption semantics (no user content).
- Backwards compatible: defaults to existing streaming behaviour when client doesn't support acks.

Protocol surface (sketch)
- transport: reuse existing streaming channel (HTTP/2 bidirectional, websocket, server-sent events) by multiplexing a tiny control frame or an out-of-band short POST to /v1/streams/:session/ack.
- frame fields: { type, seq, consumed_token_count?, target_action_id? } where: 
  - type: one of [progress_ack, prefetch_request, hold_ack, final_ack, nudge] (string)
  - seq: simple incremental client seq to reason about ordering (int as string)
  - consumed_token_count: approximate number of tokens client has rendered (int as string, optional)
  - target_action_id: when acknowledging tool output or correlating to a tool call (string, optional)

Ack semantics (high level)
- progress_ack: emitted periodically by SDK when SDK has appended the latest streamed chunk to client UI. Helps runtime decide whether to prefetch next chunks or evict KV.
- prefetch_request: client indicates it will likely request follow-on generations (e.g., user is typing). Server can opportunistically warm KV caches or spawn light speculative invocations. Must be used conservatively to avoid cost blowups.
- hold_ack: client signals it's intentionally pausing (backgrounded tab). Server can deprioritize batching but keep prefix cached for a TTL.
- final_ack: client confirms it received final chunk. Useful for billing reconciliation and for early eviction.
- nudge: client asks server to resend last partial frame (rare; recovery).

Speculative tool-calling integration
- When the runtime receives a prefetch_request with a high confidence routing (based on prompt pattern + model profiles), it may:
  - pre-warm a precomputed tool input (no external side-effects).
  - schedule a speculative tool call in a sandbox with a speculative idempotency token (spec-{uuid}). Do not hit customer data sinks until final_confirm.
- If the client later issues a confirmed tool-execute request, the runtime can fast-path by using the speculative results after validation. If speculative call produced side-effects, the runtime must ensure either it was a read-only simulation or rollback is possible.

Idempotency and safety
- All speculative actions should use a distinct speculative idempotency namespace. Only upon explicit final_ack or explicit client request should the speculative results be promoted to committed actions.
- Tool-call API must accept an optional speculative_token to allow safe promotion.

SDK ergonomics (developer-facing)
- High-level SDK will expose:
  - StreamSession.create(opts) -> session handle
  - session.on('chunk', cb), session.on('stall', cb), session.ackProgress(), session.prefetchLikely(), session.hold(), session.closeAck()
- Default SDK behavior: emit progress_ack every 200ms when new bytes are rendered; emit prefetch_request after 350ms of typing activity; send hold_ack on page visibilitychange hidden; exponential backoff for nudge retries.
- Mobile considerations: batch ack frames behind network-friendly batching (coalesce 100ms), mark acks as low-priority to avoid starving foreground calls.

Telemetry and observability
- Minimal fields we should capture server-side per-session: last_client_seq, last_consumed_token_count, prefetch_count, speculative_tool_count, final_ack_time, hold_intervals (encoded as a simple string list), client-sdk-version, transport-type.
- Tie traces: include session id and last_client_seq in span attributes so SDK-side traces can be correlated with backend spans and infra metrics.
- Suggested SLOs: 95th percentile prefetch-trigger-to-warm-state < 80ms for dedicated capacity; speculative promotion success rate > 80% for high-signal prompt patterns.

Operational concerns
- Billing: progress_ack and prefetch_request should not by themselves incur chargeable compute; only promoted speculative calls or committed tool actions are billable. We must update billing docs to explain speculative prefetch allowances.
- Abuse & spamming: clients could spam prefetch_request to force runtime work. Rate-limit prefetch_request per session and expose server-side prefetch_budget per account.
- Cache eviction: hold_ack should give a short soft-TTL boost (configurable by plan).

Compatibility & rollout plan
1) Phase 0: instrument server to accept ack frames but ignore them (no behavior change) — collect data.
2) Phase 1: SDK opt-in: new SDKs emit progress_ack and prefetch_request; server logs usage and runs experiments measuring correlation of consumed_token_count to completion rate.
3) Phase 2: enable conservative prefetch heuristics for high-repeat patterns behind feature flags (canary 5% of traffic).
4) Phase 3: full rollout with admin tunables (prefetch budgets, speculative promotion thresholds).

Open questions / TODOs
- exact wire encoding: small JSON frames vs. binary protobufs? Need perf benchmark for mobile.
- how to compute consumed_token_count reliably across different tokenizers and languages? Might be approximate.
- defensive mode for regulatory data: should speculative tool calls be disabled by default for Private deployments? (security team to advise)
- UI/UX: what should the host app show when SDK promotes speculative result? developer playbook required.

Acceptance metrics
- Improvement in measured median time-to-first-visible-next-chunk for interactive flows (target: -25ms).
- Reduced unnecessary model-compile/prefetch events per session (target: -20% wasted warms).
- Speculative promotion success rate and net cost delta (want positive net decrease in end-to-end latency without >10% increase in infra cost).

Appendix: example pseudo-SDK snippet
// JS pseudocode
const s = StreamSession.create({model: 'redwood-lite', stream: true});
s.on('chunk', (c) => { render(c); s.ackProgress(); });
// user types
input.on('typing', () => { s.prefetchLikely(); });
// visibility change
window.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => { if (document.hidden) s.hold(); else s.ackProgress(); });

Notes to reviewers: this is a UX & runtime co-design. I want early feedback from serving-runtime on safe speculative sandboxing patterns and from SDK owners on batching tradeoffs for mobile.

Slack thread: #hosted-sdk-streaming (see pinned discussion Feb 6).
Jira: PRODENG-2147 for runtime work; SDK-593 for client API changes.

-- Priya
